examples.explanation: Use vertices 0,1,2 with edges 0→2 twice, 2→1 and 1→0. Create copy 0, then copy 2 and append it twice to copy 0. Processing 2 creates copy 1; processing 1 links back to the existing copy 0. The structural judge accepts the fresh three-vertex cycle. JSON arguments [vertexCount, directedEdgePairs] construct a graph rooted at vertex 0. The callable returns the copied root; expected true records structural validation, not a boolean return.

lru_cache.description: Implement a least-recently-used cache. Initialize(capacity) or the language’s constructor starts an empty cache. Lookup returns -1 if missing and refreshes recency. Insert refreshes existing keys while preserving their old price; new insertions evict the least recent entry when full. Erase reports whether a key existed.
constraints: Capacity is nonnegative. Keys and prices are integers; initialize/construct before operations. Lookup misses return −1. Existing-key insertion refreshes recency but preserves the original price. Capacity zero stores nothing.
Lookup returns the stored price or −1; Insert returns no value; Erase returns whether the key existed. The walkthrough’s true is aggregate wrapper validation.
Each operation mutates cache membership or recency as specified. Lookup misses do not insert. Erase removes only the requested key; initialization resets state.

checks.correctness: Normalize any coin representation without increasing its count: replace five pennies by a nickel, two nickels by a dime, three dimes by a quarter and nickel, and two dimes plus a nickel by a quarter. checks.actualAlgorithm: Sort durations and pair opposite ends. Pairing the largest duration with the smallest available one minimizes the possible maximum pair sum by the exchange argument, and yields the required canonical order.
checks.correctness: Let the smallest remaining duration be s and the largest be M. If an assignment pairs M with x and s with y, replacing those pairs with (M, s) and (x, y) cannot increase the previous maximum pair sum: M + s ≤ M + x and x + y ≤ x + M. Thus an optimum exists containing the extreme pair. Repeating the argument proves the sorted opposite-end pairing is optimal and gives the required canonical order.
checks.workedTrace: Sort durations [12, 3, 8, 5, 17, 9] into [3, 5, 8, 9, 12, 17]. Pair opposite ends: (3, 17), (5, 12), (8, 9). Their sums are 20, 17 and 17. Return [[3, 17], [5, 12], [8, 9]], whose maximum pair sum is 20.
checks.edgeCases: The number of durations is even. Equal durations remain separate tasks and may create identical pairs. Two tasks make one pair; zero tasks make an empty result.
checks.timeDerivation: O(n log n) time. Sorting dominates the n/2 constant-time pair constructions.
checks.spaceDerivation: O(n) space for the sorted copy and returned pairs. The output contains n/2 pairs; C#/JavaScript and C++ also hold an O(n) sorted copy.

checks.correctness: For the unhit interval with earliest right endpoint, every feasible cover must choose some point inside it. Moving that point to its right endpoint cannot uncover any later-ending interval it previously hit. Thus selecting that endpoint is safe, and repeating on remaining unhit intervals yields a minimum cover.

checks.actualAlgorithm: Remember the last position of each word. The nearest earlier equal word is always its latest occurrence, so checking those distances suffices. Return −1 if no repeated word is found.
checks.correctness: For the current word, any earlier occurrence farther left than its latest occurrence gives a no-smaller distance. Therefore checking only the stored latest index is sufficient at every position. The minimum across those nearest predecessor distances is the global nearest repetition.
checks.workedTrace: In ["sun","rain","wind","sun","rain"], sun repeats at indices 0 and 3 and rain at indices 1 and 4. Both distances are 3, so return 3.
checks.edgeCases: Return −1 when every word is distinct. Adjacent equal words have distance 1. A word occurring many times must update its latest index after every occurrence.
checks.timeDerivation: O(n) expected One expected-constant-time hash lookup/update per word. The entry-count bound treats word hashing/comparison as constant; include examined character lengths when words are unbounded.
checks.spaceDerivation: O(number of distinct words) There is one last-index record per distinct word.

checks.actualAlgorithm: Expand a sliding window while counting its required words. Once every keyword is present, advance the left edge as far as possible, recording shorter covering windows before removing each left entry.
checks.correctness: The window counts record exactly the required-word multiplicities between left and right, and present counts the keywords with positive multiplicity. Expansion makes every possible right endpoint available. While the window covers the set, shrinking examines its shortest valid suffix before removing an indispensable word. A globally optimal interval appears during the iteration at its right endpoint, so the best recorded interval is optimal.
checks.workedTrace: For [oak, cedar, ash, oak, elm, ash] and keywords {oak, ash, elm}, the window first covers everything at indices [0, 4]. Removing oak at 0 preserves another oak at 3; removing cedar at 1 loses no keyword. This reaches [2, 4], containing ash, oak, elm in three entries. Return (2, 4); the protocol checks length 3. The callable returns inclusive zero-based endpoints. The executable walkthrough expected value is their length after the wrapper validates keyword coverage.
checks.edgeCases: Duplicate occurrences in the paragraph must not count as distinct keywords. Irrelevant words at either edge can be removed. The input set determines keyword membership; a covering interval is guaranteed by this exercise.
checks.timeDerivation: O(n + k) expected time. Each window endpoint advances at most n times after O(k) initialization. The entry-count bound treats word hashing/comparison as constant; include examined character lengths when words are unbounded.
checks.spaceDerivation: O(k) auxiliary space for keyword counts. At most k keyword counts are stored.

checks.actualAlgorithm: For each distinct keyword, track the latest possible starting index of a prefix of the required sequence. A matching later keyword extends the preceding prefix. Whenever the final keyword matches, compare the resulting interval with the best seen.
checks.correctness: For each keyword position j, start[j] stores the latest starting position of a valid sequence of keywords 0 through j in the processed paragraph. The first keyword starts a new prefix; a later keyword can extend only a previously completed preceding prefix. Keeping the latest start minimizes the length for any fixed ending position. Checking every occurrence of the final keyword therefore finds a globally shortest covering interval.
checks.workedTrace: Use paragraph [elm, oak, cedar, elm, oak, ash, pine] and ordered keywords [elm, oak, ash]. The first elm/oak prefix starts at 0. The elm at index 3 replaces its start, and oak at 4 extends that newer prefix. Ash at 5 completes indices [3, 5], a three-word interval. The method returns (3, 5); the existing judge reports its length, 3. The callable returns inclusive zero-based endpoints. The executable walkthrough expected value is their length after the wrapper checks the required keyword sequence.
checks.edgeCases: Keywords are distinct and the supplied corpus guarantees a covering interval. Repeated paragraph matches must allow a newer, shorter prefix to replace an older one. A single keyword gives a one-entry interval; ties may use any shortest valid interval.

checks.spaceDerivation: O(k) auxiliary space. There are O(k) keyword indices and prefix states.

With one zero, excluding another entry leaves product zero while excluding that zero gives the nonzero product. With two or more zeros every exclusion still leaves a zero. Taking the maximum among these exhaustive possibilities is optimal.

checks.actualAlgorithm: Split after the middle node, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves alternately. All links are rearranged on the original nodes, including the odd-length middle node.
checks.correctness: Splitting leaves the first half in original order and the second half with the remaining suffix. Reversing that suffix exposes the original last node first, then the second-last, and so on. Alternately linking one node from each half therefore yields exactly L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1, ... . The halves are disjoint and terminated before weaving, so each original node appears once without a cycle.
checks.workedTrace: For [4, 8, 15, 23, 42, 57], split into [4, 8, 15] and [23, 42, 57]. Reverse the second half to [57, 42, 23]. Weave the halves as 4, 57, 8, 42, 15, 23. Return [4, 57, 8, 42, 15, 23]. JSON arrays describe list node values. The callable returns a node head; expected is the sequence reached by following its next links.
checks.edgeCases: Null and one-node lists are already zipped. An odd-length list keeps its unpaired middle node exactly once. The original node objects and values are reused; the first half is terminated before reversing and weaving.
checks.timeDerivation: O(n) time. Finding the split, reversing the suffix and weaving each traverse O(n) links.
checks.spaceDerivation: O(1) auxiliary space; original nodes are reused. Only a constant number of node references are retained; existing nodes are reused.

checks.actualAlgorithm: Give everyone one bonus. A left-to-right pass enforces each left-neighbor constraint; a right-to-left pass raises bonuses only where the right-neighbor constraint demands it. The maximum of these lower bounds is the minimum valid allocation.
checks.correctness: The forward pass gives the least bonuses satisfying every rising left-neighbor constraint. The backward pass raises bonuses only to satisfy rising right-neighbor constraints. Every valid solution must meet both lower bounds, so taking their maximum at each position is feasible and minimal.
checks.workedTrace: For productivity [2,5,3], start at [1,1,1]. The forward pass raises the middle bonus to 2; the reverse pass needs no further increase. The minimum total is 1+2+1=4.
checks.edgeCases: Equal productivity creates no strict bonus requirement. Strictly decreasing sequences are handled by the reverse pass. Every employee receives at least one.

Duplicates lie on every line through that anchor and are added to each direction’s count. Choosing the earliest supplied point on an optimal line ensures its pass counts every entry on that line.
checks.workedTrace: For [(0,0),(0,0),(2,2),(4,4),(0,3)], the anchor (0,0) has one duplicate plus two points in direction (1,1). Including the anchor gives 4 entries on the diagonal; the last point is off that line.
checks.edgeCases: Repeated coordinates count as separate entries. Vertical lines normalize to a single direction. Opposite directions must represent the same anchored line.
checks.timeDerivation: O(n² log C), where C bounds coordinate differences There are O(n²) anchor/other-point pairs; normalizing each direction uses a gcd taking O(log C) steps for coordinate difference bound C.
checks.spaceDerivation: O(n) One anchor’s slope map has at most n entries and is discarded before the next anchor.
checks.callableAgreement: Callable: function findLineWithMostPoints(points). Signed 32-bit integer (x,y) coordinates. Duplicate entries count separately. Empty input gives zero; a singleton gives one. Do not approximate slope equality using rounded floating-point division. Return the value specified by the description; ties between equivalent witnesses do not change this scalar result. The callable reads its input; no caller-visible mutation is needed for this result.
